abstract: Sex differences influence human physiology and disease susceptibility, yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying sex-biased transcription remain unclear. Here we present eModule, which quantifies enhancer RNA (eRNA) transcription from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) RNA-seq data to identify sex-biased active enhancers across 41 human tissues. We find that 47% of transcriptionally active enhancers are sex-biased in at least one tissue. These enhancers are tissue-specific, often organized into super-enhancers with chromatin signatures, and associated with rewiring of transcription factor (TF) regulatory networks. Evolutionary analyses reveal that many sex-biased enhancers are primate-specific and derived from transposable element (TE) exaptation, with contributing TE families enriched for binding sites of sex-associated TFs. Sex-biased enhancers also harbor variants linked to traits with sex differences and are inferred to regulate therapeutic target genes. Our findings position sex-biased enhancer activity as a regulatory layer shaping sex-biased transcription, with implications for regulatory evolution, GWAS interpretation, and sex-informed precision medicine.
